blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 6 (Chemical Energetics), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define enthalpy and enthalpy change. Explain exothermic and endothermic processes in terms of HP and HR, with one example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Enthalpy (heat content), H: the energy possessed by a substance due to its structure (types of bonds) and physical state.

Enthalpy change, ΔH: every substance has a characteristic enthalpy, so the total enthalpy of products (HP) is never equal to that of reactants (HR). The net energy evolved or absorbed as heat is the enthalpy change:
ΔH = HP – HR

Exothermic process (HP < HR): a chemical reaction or physical change in which heat is evolved from the system to the surroundings. Enthalpy is lowered and ΔH is negative.
Example: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = –393.7 kJ mol⁻¹

Endothermic process (HP > HR): a chemical reaction or physical change in which heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings. Enthalpy increases and ΔH is positive.
Example: NH₄Cl(s) + H₂O(l) → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), ΔH = +16.2 kJ mol⁻¹ (used in cold packs).

book_ref.quote: In other words, enthalpy change is the net energy

blocks.prompt: 2 What is energy of activation? Describe the energy profile diagrams of an exothermic and an endothermic reaction. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
All chemical reactions involve breaking of bonds in the reactant molecules before new bonds are formed. This is possible only if reactant molecules collide with a sufficient amount of energy to overcome an energy barrier.

Energy of activation, Ea: the minimum amount of energy required by the reactant molecules just to cross that energy barrier.

Energy profile diagram (Figure 6.2): energy is plotted against the progress of the reaction. The curve rises from the reactants to the top of the barrier (height = Ea) and then falls to the products.
• Exothermic reaction: the products lie below the reactants; the difference is ΔH, which is negative (heat evolved).
• Endothermic reaction: the products lie above the reactants; ΔH is positive (heat absorbed).
In both cases the reactants must first gain energy Ea before products are formed.

book_ref.quote: This can be achieved only if the reactant molecules collide

blocks.prompt: 3 What are standard conditions? Define the standard enthalpy changes of reaction, formation, combustion and atomization, giving one equation for each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The enthalpy of a substance depends on its physical state, pressure and temperature, so for accurate comparison ΔH is measured under standard conditions: temperature 25 °C (298 K) and pressure 1 atm (101 kPa). The standard state of an element is its most stable form at 298 K and 1 atm (carbon: graphite).

Standard enthalpy of reaction: the enthalpy change when stoichiometric amounts of reactants in their standard states react together completely to form products under standard conditions.
H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔHr = –286 kJ mol⁻¹

Standard enthalpy change of formation: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions (exothermic or endothermic; zero for an element in its standard state).
C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g), ΔH°f = –74.8 kJ mol⁻¹

Standard enthalpy change of combustion: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burnt in excess of oxygen under standard conditions (always exothermic).
C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), ΔH°c = –1368 kJ mol⁻¹

Standard enthalpy change of atomization: the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element under standard conditions.
½H₂(g) → H(g), ΔH°at = +218 kJ mol⁻¹

book_ref.quote: when making accurate comparisons of enthalpy changes for various reactions

blocks.prompt: 4 Define standard enthalpy change of neutralization. Explain why its value for all strong acid–strong base reactions is nearly the same, and define first electron affinity. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Standard enthalpy change of neutralization: the enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with an alkali under standard conditions. It is always exothermic; for NaOH with HCl it is –57.1 kJ mol⁻¹.

Why nearly constant: strong acids and alkalis are completely ionized in solution. When NaOH(aq) and HCl(aq) are mixed, the only change is the formation of water molecules; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ remain as free ions:
Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
Net: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH°n = –57.1 kJ mol⁻¹
So the enthalpy of neutralization is merely the heat of formation of one mole of liquid water from its ions, and for all strong acid–base reactions ΔH°n is near –57.1 kJ mol⁻¹.

First electron affinity: the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions under standard conditions. Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻, ΔH = –348.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (energy released, negative sign).

book_ref.quote: When these solutions are mixed together during the process of neutralization

blocks.prompt: 5 Define bond dissociation energy. Explain exact and average bond energies with the example of the C–C bond in ethane, propane and butane. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
When a bond is formed between two atoms, energy is released; the same amount is absorbed when the bond is broken to form neutral atoms.

Bond dissociation energy (E): the average amount of energy required to break (dissociate) one mole of a particular bond in a substance.

Exact bond energy: the bond energy of a particular bond in a particular substance. Bonds between the same pair of atoms have different values in different compounds, because B.E. is affected by the other atoms in the molecule:
In ethane, H₃C–CH₃: EC–C = 376 kJ mol⁻¹
In propane, H₃C–CH₂–CH₃: EC–C = 356 kJ mol⁻¹
In butane, H₃C–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃: EC–C = 352 kJ mol⁻¹
Each of these is an exact bond energy.

Average bond energy: the average of EC–C over different molecules. C–C bonds usually have values of about 350 to 380 kJ mol⁻¹. Practically, average bond energies (Table 6.1) are used instead of exact ones.

book_ref.quote: This is to be noted that bonds between the same pair of atoms usually have different B.E. values

blocks.prompt: 6 Explain how the enthalpy change of a reaction comes from the breaking and forming of chemical bonds. Use the formation of water as an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A chemical reaction is a process in which old bonds are broken and new bonds are formed, so ΔHr comes from bond breaking and bond forming. A chemical bond is a form of chemical energy.

• Bond breaking absorbs energy (ΔH = +ve).
• Bond formation releases energy (ΔH = –ve).
Their difference decides the overall sign of ΔH:
• Exothermic: energy released in making new bonds > energy absorbed in breaking bonds.
• Endothermic: energy absorbed in breaking bonds > energy released in making bonds.

Example, formation of water: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g), ΔHr = –ve
Energy is needed to break the H–H bonds and the O=O bond, while energy is released in making the H–O bonds of water. More energy is released in forming the H–O bonds than is absorbed in breaking H–H and O=O, so the reaction is exothermic.
In general ΔH°r = ΣER – ΣEP; e.g. for H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(g) with EH–H = 436, EO=O = 495, EH–O = 463 kJ mol⁻¹: ΔH = (436 + 247.5) – 926 = –242.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: That is whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic is determined by the net change.

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the glass calorimeter. How is the enthalpy change of a reaction calculated from it? State its limitations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Construction (Figure 6.3): a beaker, a stirrer, a thermometer and a loose-fitting lid that keeps the contents at atmospheric pressure. The outside walls are insulated with cotton wool to minimize heat exchange with the surrounding air.

Working: the reaction is carried out inside the beaker; the heat evolved or absorbed is measured by the temperature change. Since the pressure is constant, this gives the enthalpy change ΔH.

Calculation: all the heat stays in the calorimeter and is absorbed by water, so
1. q = mwater × cwater × ΔT (c of water = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; dilute solutions are almost all water, so c of water is used)
2. Convert q into kJ by dividing by 1000.
3. ΔH = –q/n kJ mol⁻¹ (for an exothermic reaction), i.e. ΔH = –mcΔT/n, where n = number of moles.

Limitations: suitable for reactions in solution (e.g. heat of neutralization); it cannot be used for reactions involving gases, which would escape from the vessel, or for reactions in which the products reach high temperatures.

book_ref.quote: The reaction is carried out inside the beaker and the heat evolved or absorbed is measured by the temperature change.

blocks.prompt: 8 75 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl at 25.0 °C is mixed with 75 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 25.0 °C in a glass calorimeter. The temperature rises to 31.8 °C. Calculate the enthalpy of neutralization (density of solution 1 g cm⁻³, c = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find q from m c ΔT for the whole mixture, find the moles of water formed, then ΔH°n = –q/n.

book_ref.quote: Find the enthalpy of neutralization. Specific heat of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹K⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 9 2.14 g of NH₄Cl (molar mass 53.5 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 50.0 g of water in a calorimeter. The temperature falls from 25.00 °C to 21.90 °C. Calculate (i) the heat absorbed from the water, (ii) ΔH for the dissolution of NH₄Cl (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: The temperature falls, so the process is endothermic: the heat lost by the water is absorbed by the dissolving salt, and ΔH = +q/n.

book_ref.quote: ΔT is the temperature change in °C

steps: q = c × m × ΔT = 4.18 × 50.0 × 3.10 = 647.9 J = 0.648 kJ absorbed from the water

blocks.prompt: 10 Ethanol burns according to C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), ΔH°c = –1368 kJ mol⁻¹. Taking the molar mass of ethanol as 46 g mol⁻¹ and 4.184 kJ = 1 kcal, calculate (i) ΔH per gram, (ii) the calorie content in kcal/g, (iii) the energy released by 10 g of ethanol. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Divide ΔH per mole by the molar mass to get ΔH per gram, then divide by 4.184 kJ/kcal (calorie content = –ΔH/4.184, a positive number).

book_ref.quote: First, we find ΔH per gram of glucose.

steps: ΔH per gram = –1368 kJ mol⁻¹ ÷ 46 g mol⁻¹ = –29.74 kJ g⁻¹
Energy from 10 g = 10 g × 29.74 kJ g⁻¹ = 297.4 kJ (or 10/46 mol × 1368 kJ mol⁻¹ = 297.4 kJ)

blocks.prompt: 11 State Hess's law of heat summation and show its relation to the law of conservation of energy. Illustrate it with a Hess cycle having a direct route and two indirect routes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, but can be converted from one form to another. The first law of thermodynamics is a manifestation of this law; Germain Henri Hess applied it to enthalpy changes.

Hess's law: the total enthalpy change in a chemical reaction is independent of the route by which the reaction takes place, as long as the initial and final conditions are the same.

Hess cycle (Figure 6.4): A is converted to B
• directly in a single step (direct route), ΔHr;
• by indirect route 1, in two steps ΔH₁ and ΔH₂;
• by indirect route 2, in three steps ΔH₃, ΔH₄ and ΔH₅.
The products formed in these routes (M, N and X, Y, Z) are reaction intermediates. According to Hess's law:
Indirect route 1: ΔHr = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂
Indirect route 2: ΔHr = ΔH₃ + ΔH₄ + ΔH₅

Importance: for many reactions ΔH cannot be measured directly by calorimetry, e.g. CCl₄ cannot be prepared directly from carbon and chlorine; Hess's law lets us calculate such enthalpy changes.

book_ref.quote: Let A be converted to ‘B’ directly in a single step, which is the direct route

blocks.prompt: 12 When 4.00 g of methane, CH₄ (16.0 g mol⁻¹), is burned in excess oxygen, 222.6 kJ of heat is evolved: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Given ΔH°f[CO₂(g)] = –393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH°f[H₂O(l)] = –285.8 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of methane. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: First find ΔH°c per mole of methane, then apply Hess's law: ΔHr = ΣΔH°f(products) – ΣΔH°f(reactants), with ΔH°f(O₂) = 0.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of propane.

blocks.final_answer: ΔH°f(CH₄) = –74.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (close to the chapter's –74.8 kJ mol⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 13 For C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), calculate ΔH°r (i) from enthalpies of formation, ΔH°f(C₂H₄) = +52.2 and ΔH°f(C₂H₆) = –84.7 kJ mol⁻¹, and (ii) from the average bond energies EC=C = 615, EC–C = 348, EC–H = 413 and EH–H = 436 kJ mol⁻¹. Why do the two answers differ? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use ΣΔH°f(products) – ΣΔH°f(reactants) for (i), and ΣER – ΣEP for (ii); only the bonds that change need to be counted.

book_ref.quote: The enthalpy change for this step can be calculated by adding the bond enthalpies from Table 6.1.

steps: (ii) Bonds broken: one C=C + one H–H = 615 + 436 = 1051 kJ (the four C–H bonds of C₂H₄ remain)
Bonds formed: one C–C + two new C–H = 348 + 2(413) = 1174 kJ
The values differ because (ii) uses average bond energies, not the exact bond energies in these molecules, so it is only an estimate.
blocks.final_answer: (i) –136.9 kJ mol⁻¹; (ii) –123 kJ mol⁻¹ (estimate from average bond energies)

blocks.prompt: 14 Use bond energies from Table 6.1 (EN≡N = 945, EH–H = 436, EN–H = 391 kJ mol⁻¹) to estimate ΔH for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), and hence the enthalpy of formation of NH₃(g). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Replace the reaction by two steps: break all reactant bonds to give gaseous atoms (ΣER), then form the product bonds (ΣEP); ΔH = ΣER – ΣEP, then divide by 2 for one mole of NH₃.

book_ref.quote: And finally calculate the heat of formation of HCl.

steps: Step 2: 2N(g) + 6H(g) → 2NH₃(g); six N–H bonds formed: ΣEP = 6(391) = 2346 kJ
ΔHr = ΣER – ΣEP = 2253 – 2346 = –93 kJ (for 2 mol NH₃)
blocks.final_answer: ΔHr = –93 kJ; ΔH°f(NH₃) ≈ –46.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (the chapter's measured value is –45.9 kJ mol⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 15 Define dissolution and standard enthalpy of solution. Describe the three steps of solution formation and the two factors that govern the dissolution of an ionic compound. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Dissolution: the process of dissolving a solute in a solvent.

Standard enthalpy of solution, ΔH°sol: the amount of heat absorbed or evolved when one mole of a substance is dissolved in a solvent to give an infinitely dilute solution. It may be exothermic or endothermic:
Na₂CO₃(s) + aq → 2Na⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq), ΔH°sol = –25 kJ mol⁻¹
NH₄Cl(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), ΔH°sol = +16.2 kJ mol⁻¹

Three steps (assumed):
1. Overcoming the intermolecular forces in the solvent to make room for the solute (expanding the solvent).
2. Breaking up the solute into individual components (expanding the solute).
3. Allowing the solute and solvent to interact to form the solution.
In this process heat is given out or taken in.

Two factors for an ionic compound (oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces):
• Lattice energy, which controls the breaking of the ionic compound;
• Hydration energy, which accounts for the attraction of the solute ions with water molecules.

book_ref.quote: In this process heat is either given out or taken in.

blocks.prompt: 16 What is hydration? Explain the factors that affect the magnitude of hydration energy, with examples of the order of hydration enthalpies. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hydration: when ionic compounds dissolve in water they dissociate into ions; the process in which water molecules surround and interact with the solute ions is hydration. The forces between water molecules and ions are ion-dipole forces (Figure 6.5), and the ions are said to be hydrated.

Enthalpy of hydration, ΔHhyd: the energy of attraction due to ion-dipole forces. It is always released, as ion-dipole bonds are formed.

Factors:
1. Charge on the ion
2. Size of the ion
These are combined as charge density (charge per unit area). A greater charge on a smaller ion gives a large charge density; such ions are strongly attracted by water molecules, so the hydration energy is greater.

Examples:
• Na⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Al³⁺: charge increases and size decreases, so hydration energy increases.
• Mg²⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Sr²⁺: same charge, size increases down the group, so hydration energy decreases.
The hydration energy of anions is explained on the same basis.

book_ref.quote: For example, enthalpies of hydration of following ions are in the order:

blocks.prompt: 17 Define lattice energy. Explain how the charge and the size of the ions affect the magnitude of lattice energy, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Lattice energy, ΔHlatt: the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from gaseous ions under standard conditions. It is released, so it is negative:
Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s), ΔH°latt = –787 kJ mol⁻¹

1. Charge on the ions: lattice energy increases with the magnitude of the charges on the ions. LiF and MgO have the same arrangement of ions and comparable ion sizes; the major difference is ionic charge.
ΔHlatt[MgO] = –3923 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔHlatt[LiF] = –1049 kJ mol⁻¹
Doubly charged Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ attract each other more strongly than singly charged ions of the same size; greater charge means higher charge density and stronger ionic bonds.

2. Size of the ions: for the alkali metal halides (Figure 6.6) lattice energy decreases as the size of the cation or anion increases, because larger ions pack less tightly, so the attraction between oppositely charged ions is weaker.

book_ref.quote: Let us try to understand this fact by comparing lithium fluoride, LiF, with magnesium oxide, MgO.

blocks.prompt: 18 Explain, in terms of lattice energy and hydration energy, the solubility trends of the Group II hydroxides and sulphates. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
ΔH°sol depends on both lattice energy and hydration enthalpy (ΔH°sol = ΔH°hyd – ΔH°latt).

Group II hydroxides, Mg(OH)₂ → Ba(OH)₂:
• Both hydration energy of the cations and lattice energy decrease down the group, because the charge density of the Group 2 cations decreases.
• The lattice energy decreases more rapidly in the series Mg(OH)₂, Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂ than the hydration energy of Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺.
• The lattice energy factor dominates; ΔH°sol becomes more exothermic, so solubility increases down the group.

Group II sulphates, MgSO₄ → BaSO₄:
• The sulphate ion, SO₄²⁻, is much larger than OH⁻, so the decrease in lattice energy from MgSO₄ to BaSO₄ is small.
• The hydration energy of the cation decreases by a greater amount.
• The hydration energy dominates; ΔH°sol becomes more endothermic, so solubility decreases from MgSO₄ to BaSO₄.

book_ref.quote: Look at the solubility trends of group II metal hydroxides.

blocks.prompt: 19 Using an enthalpy cycle, calculate the standard enthalpy change of solution of KCl from: lattice energy of KCl = –718 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH°hyd(K⁺) = –322 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔH°hyd(Cl⁻) = –378 kJ mol⁻¹. Is the dissolution exothermic or endothermic? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Draw the cycle gaseous ions → solid (ΔH°latt), solid → aqueous ions (ΔH°sol), gaseous ions → aqueous ions (ΔH°hyd); Hess's law gives ΔH°latt + ΔH°sol = ΔH°hyd.

book_ref.quote: Determine the enthalpy change of solution

steps: Cycle: K⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → KCl(s) (ΔH°latt); KCl(s) + aq → K⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) (ΔH°sol); K⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) + aq → K⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) (ΔH°hyd)
ΔH°latt + ΔH°sol = ΔH°hyd, so ΔH°sol = ΔH°hyd – ΔH°latt
blocks.final_answer: ΔH°sol(KCl) = +18 kJ mol⁻¹: endothermic (Table 6.2 gives 17.8 kJ mol⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 20 Why is the Born-Haber cycle needed? Describe the Born-Haber cycle for sodium chloride, naming each step and writing the relation used to find ΔH°latt. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Need: the lattice energy of a compound cannot be determined by a single direct experiment. It is calculated from several experimental data using an energy cycle, the Born-Haber cycle, which is an application of Hess's law.

Energy triangle: Na(s) + ½Cl₂(g) → Na⁺Cl⁻(s) directly (ΔH°f, measured in a calorimeter), or first to gaseous ions Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) (ΔHx) and then to the solid (ΔH°latt):
ΔHx + ΔH°latt = ΔH°f

Stages of ΔHx (Figure 6.9):
1. Atomization of sodium: Na(s) → Na(g), ΔH°at(Na)
2. First ionization of sodium: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻, ΔH°i1(Na)
3. Atomization of chlorine: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g), ΔH°at(Cl)
4. First electron affinity of chlorine: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g), ΔH°ea1(Cl)
ΔHx = ΔH°at(Na) + ΔH°i1(Na) + ΔH°at(Cl) + ΔH°ea1(Cl) = 376 kJ mol⁻¹
5. Gaseous ions form the solid: Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s), ΔH°latt

Hence ΔH°latt = ΔH°f – ΔHx = –787 kJ mol⁻¹ for NaCl.

book_ref.quote: The above energy triangle has been extended to show the various stages involved in finding ΔHx.

blocks.prompt: 21 Calculate the lattice energy of lithium fluoride using the Born-Haber cycle: ΔH°f(LiF) = –616, ΔH°at(Li) = +159, ΔH°i1(Li) = +520, ΔH°at(F) (½ bond energy of F₂) = +79, ΔH°ea1(F) = –328 kJ mol⁻¹. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add the steps that turn Li(s) and ½F₂(g) into gaseous ions to get ΔHx, then use ΔH°latt = ΔH°f – ΔHx.

book_ref.quote: Solution: Values are given for all the quantities in the Born-Haber cycle

steps: ΔHx + ΔH°latt = ΔH°f, so ΔH°latt = ΔH°f – ΔHx
blocks.final_answer: ΔH°latt(LiF) = –1046 kJ mol⁻¹ (close to the chapter's –1049 kJ mol⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 22 Define entropy. Explain entropy in terms of diffusion and the number of ways of arrangement of molecules in two connected jars. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Entropy: a measure of the number of ways energy can be distributed within a system at a specific temperature. When energy is distributed in more ways, the system is more stable. Entropy is also a measure of randomness or disorder: the higher the disorder, the greater the entropy.

Diffusion model (Figure 6.10): molecules of a vapour diffuse by chance. Jar A containing molecules is connected to an empty jar B; when the stopcock is opened each molecule can be in either jar.
• Number of molecules in A = 3, number of jars = 2: arrangements = 2³ = 8
• With 5 molecules: 2⁵ = 32
• With 100 molecules: 2¹⁰⁰
General formula: xʸ, where x = number of places and y = number of particles.

Diffusion happens because there is a large number of ways of arranging the molecules once they can spread over both jars. The idea of the number of ways of arranging particles, or the energy within them, helps predict whether a change can happen.

book_ref.quote: Consider the simplified model shown in Figure 6.10 below.

blocks.prompt: 23 How can the entropies of substances be compared? State the rules for predicting the entropy change of a reaction, with two examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Comparison of entropy values:
• Number of particles: a small number of particles means low entropy; CaCO₃ (92.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) > CaO (39.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
• Hardness (similar chemical nature): harder substances have lower entropy; diamond < graphite, because strong forces limit vibrations.
• Physical state: solid < liquid < gas; ice 48.0, water 69.9, water vapour 188.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

Rules for a reaction (ΔS° positive when):
1. A solid is converted to a liquid or a gas in the products.
2. The number of moles in the products is greater.
3. The number of gaseous molecules increases (gases have high entropy; more gas molecules, more ways of arranging them).

Examples:
CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g): a gas is produced from a solid, so entropy increases.
2N₂O₅(g) → 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g): 5 moles of gas from 2 moles, so entropy increases.
A positive ΔS alone does not decide spontaneity: CaCO₃ decomposition is not spontaneous at room temperature.

book_ref.quote: The following rules must be followed to know about the change in entropy of a reaction

blocks.prompt: 24 Calculate ΔS°system for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), given S°[H₂(g)] = 130.6, S°[O₂(g)] = 205.0 and S°[H₂O(l)] = 69.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Explain the sign, and why the reaction can still be feasible. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use ΔS°system = ΣnS°(products) – ΣnS°(reactants), multiplying each S° by its coefficient.

book_ref.quote: We know, however, that calcium reacts spontaneously with oxygen.

steps: Negative: 3 moles of gas form a liquid, so disorder decreases. The reaction can still be feasible because the entropy of the surroundings also plays a part; the total entropy change must be positive.
blocks.final_answer: ΔS°system = –326.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (entropy of the system decreases)

blocks.prompt: 25 What is Gibbs free energy? Derive the relation ΔG = ΔH – TΔS and explain how the sign of ΔG predicts the spontaneity of a process. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The heat content (enthalpy, H) of a system is a combination of:
• the part that is free to be converted to other forms of energy, called Gibbs free energy, G;
• the part needed to maintain the system at the specified temperature, unavailable for conversion, T × S.
H = G + TS
So all of the enthalpy would be available only at zero kelvin (TS = 0).

Derivation: for a change between two states,
ΔH = ΔG + Δ(TS)
At constant temperature, Δ(TS) = TΔS:
ΔH = ΔG + TΔS, or ΔG = ΔH – TΔS (constant T)

Spontaneity from the sign of ΔG:
• ΔG < 0 (–ve): the process may occur spontaneously.
• ΔG > 0 (+ve): the process cannot occur spontaneously; the reverse may occur.
• ΔG = 0: neither the process nor its reverse occurs spontaneously; the system is at equilibrium.
Free energy is needed because, for some reactions, the entropy change alone fails to tell about spontaneity.

blocks.prompt: 26 For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) at 25 °C, calculate ΔH°, ΔS° and ΔG° and discuss its spontaneity. Data: ΔH°f[H₂O(l)] = –286 kJ mol⁻¹; S°[H₂(g)] = 130.6, S°[O₂(g)] = 205.0, S°[H₂O(l)] = 69.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ΔH° from enthalpies of formation (elements = 0), ΔS° from standard entropies, convert ΔS° to kJ K⁻¹, then ΔG° = ΔH° – TΔS° at 298 K.

book_ref.quote: Also discuss its spontaneity.

steps: ΔG° is negative, so the reaction is spontaneous at 25 °C, even though ΔS° is negative; the large negative ΔH° outweighs –TΔS°.
blocks.final_answer: ΔH° = –572 kJ, ΔS° = –326.4 J K⁻¹, ΔG° = –474.7 kJ: spontaneous at 25 °C

blocks.prompt: 27 For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹. Given S°[CaCO₃(s)] = 92.9, S°[CaO(s)] = 39.7 and S°[CO₂(g)] = 213.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, calculate ΔS° and ΔG° at 298 K, and the temperature above which the decomposition becomes spontaneous (take ΔH° and ΔS° as constant). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ΔS°, then ΔG° = ΔH° – TΔS°; the reaction turns spontaneous when TΔS° exceeds ΔH°, i.e. above T = ΔH°/ΔS° (where ΔG° = 0).

book_ref.quote: Quick Check 6.9 (b)(v) rightly treats limestone decomposing at room temperature as not spontaneous.

steps: ΔG°(298 K) = 178 – 298(0.1604) = 178 – 47.8 = +130.2 kJ mol⁻¹: positive, so not spontaneous at room temperature
Above about 1110 K, TΔS° > ΔH° and ΔG° becomes negative, so the decomposition becomes spontaneous.
blocks.final_answer: ΔS° = +160.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔG°(298 K) = +130.2 kJ mol⁻¹ (non-spontaneous); spontaneous above about 1110 K
